prompt: "As a nurse in this emergency room for twelve years, I have treated dozens of teens injured in this exact kind of crash."

options.feedback: The speaker's experience and role build credibility. It also hints at evidence, but its main work is establishing why we should trust her.
There is emotional weight, but the sentence leads with her credentials and experience.
"Dozens" is not specific data. The appeal rests on who she is.

prompt: "Picture your little sister at a bus stop after dark: phone dead, no streetlight, the next bus forty minutes away."

options.feedback: Nothing here builds the speaker's credibility.
Vivid imagery invites listeners to feel protective concern. Ethical pathos fits the facts; if bus stops really lack lighting, this is fair.
No evidence or reasoning is offered yet.

prompt: "According to the district's annual report, students who finished the tutoring program raised their reading scores by an average of two grade levels."

options.feedback: Citing the district adds some credibility, but the sentence's main job is presenting evidence.
This is data, not an emotional appeal.
A specific, sourced result supports a claim. Notice the oral citation, which also builds ethos.

prompt: "I'll be honest: I opposed this idea last year. Reading the research changed my mind."

options.feedback: Admitting a change of mind shows honesty and open-mindedness, which builds character and goodwill. Skeptical listeners may trust a speaker who once stood where they stand.
It may create connection, but its main work is showing the speaker's fairness.
It refers to research but presents none.

prompt: "If each of our 1,200 students skips one bottled drink a week, that's more than 60,000 fewer bottles a year."

options.feedback: This sentence does not focus on the speaker.
The big number may impress, but the appeal is reasoning from a calculation.
It reasons from a clear calculation (1,200 × 52 = 62,400). Logos can make a small action feel significant.

prompt: "This park is where my grandfather taught me to fish, and where I hope my own kids will learn someday."

options.feedback: It shows a personal connection, which helps credibility, but the main pull is emotional.
Family, memory, and hope connect the park to values the audience may share. A strong speech would pair this with evidence (logos).
There is no data or reasoning here.

prompt: "Three independent research teams, using different methods, reached the same conclusion."

options.feedback: It borrows credibility from researchers, but the point is the strength of the evidence.
There is no emotional appeal here.
Converging evidence from independent sources strengthens reasoning. In a real speech, name at least one of the teams.

prompt: "My opponent has never even lived in this neighborhood, so why should we listen to her plan?"

options.text: Ethos, used to attack the other speaker's credibility
options.feedback: It targets the opponent's credibility. Be careful: dismissing an argument because of who makes it, instead of answering it, is the ad hominem fallacy (Section 14.4).
It offers no evidence about the plan itself.
It may stir resentment, but its target is the opponent's credibility.
